cases.sentence: ___ болит, так вот пускай же ее еще крепче болит.
cases.translation: My liver aches, well then let it ache even harder.
cases.explain: Печенка is the subject of болит (aches), so it stands in the nominative.

cases.sentence: буду сам на себя скрежетать зубами и от ___ несколько месяцев страдать бессонницей.
cases.translation: I'll gnash my teeth at myself and suffer from insomnia for months out of shame.
cases.explain: The preposition от (from/out of) governs the genitive case, hence стыда.

cases.sentence: Когда к ___, у которого я сидел, подходили, бывало, просители за справками, я зубами на них скрежетал.
cases.translation: When petitioners for information would approach the desk at which I sat, I would gnash my teeth at them.
cases.explain: The preposition к (toward) always governs the dative case, hence столу.

cases.sentence: У меня с ним полтора года за эту ___ война была.
cases.translation: He and I were at war for a year and a half over that saber.
cases.explain: The preposition за expressing cause ("over/because of") governs the accusative case, hence саблю.

cases.sentence: Дайте мне чайку с ___, я, пожалуй, успокоюсь.
cases.translation: Give me some tea with a bit of sugar, and I'll probably calm down.
cases.explain: The preposition с meaning "with" governs the instrumental case here, hence сахарцем.

cases.sentence: Я, разумеется, не сумею вам объяснить, кому именно я насолю в этом ___ моей злостью.
cases.translation: Of course, I won't manage to explain to you whom exactly I'm spiting with my malice in this case.
cases.explain: The preposition в indicating a static circumstance ("in this case") governs the prepositional case, hence случае.

reading.ru: Я человек больной. Я злой человек. Непривлекательный я человек.
reading.question: How does the narrator describe himself in the opening lines?
options: As a sick, spiteful, and unattractive man
As a healthy, kind, and popular man
As a wealthy and admired nobleman
As a cheerful and carefree young man
reading.correct: As a sick, spiteful, and unattractive man
reading.explain: The narrator opens by calling himself a sick man, a spiteful man, and an unattractive man.

reading.ru: Я думаю, что у меня болит печень. Впрочем, я ни шиша, ни смысла в моей болезни.
reading.question: What does the narrator admit about his illness?
options: He thinks his liver hurts, but understands nothing about the illness
He knows exactly which disease he has
He has already been fully cured
He denies being ill at all
reading.correct: He thinks his liver hurts, but understands nothing about the illness
reading.explain: He says he thinks his liver aches, but admits he understands not a thing about his own illness.

reading.ru: Хотя медицину и докторов уважаю. К тому же я еще и суеверен до крайности.
reading.question: What contradictory attitudes does the narrator confess about medicine and superstition?
options: He respects medicine and doctors, yet is extremely superstitious
He despises medicine but trusts only doctors
He believes in nothing at all, medicine or superstition
He is a doctor himself but does not believe in medicine
reading.correct: He respects medicine and doctors, yet is extremely superstitious
reading.explain: He says he respects medicine and doctors, and adds that he is also superstitious to an extreme degree.

reading.ru: Печенка болит, так вот пускай же ее еще крепче болит.
reading.question: What spiteful attitude does the narrator take toward his own aching liver?
options: He wishes it to ache even harder, out of spite
He begs it to stop hurting immediately
He ignores it and forgets about it
He is grateful for the pain
reading.correct: He wishes it to ache even harder, out of spite
reading.explain: He says spitefully, "let it ache even harder," refusing to treat his liver.

reading.ru: Я уже давно не так живу, лет 20. Теперь мне 40.
reading.question: How old is the narrator now, according to this passage?
reading.correct: Forty
reading.explain: He says he has lived this way for about 20 years and that he is now 40.

reading.ru: Я был злой чиновник. Я был груб и находил в этом удовольствие.
reading.question: What kind of official was the narrator, and how did he feel about it?
options: A spiteful official who took pleasure in being rude
A kind official loved by everyone
An official who was fired for laziness
An official who never interacted with the public
reading.correct: A spiteful official who took pleasure in being rude
reading.explain: He says he was a spiteful official and found pleasure in being rude.

reading.ru: Ведь я взяток не брал. Стало быть, должен же был себя хоть этим вознаградить.
reading.question: What one thing does the narrator claim never to have done as an official, which he used to reward himself?
reading.correct: Taking bribes
reading.explain: He says he never took bribes, and had to reward himself somehow for that virtue.

reading.ru: Когда к столу, у которого я сидел, подходили, бывало, просители за справками, я зубами на них скрежетал и чувствовал, Неумолимое наслаждение, когда удавалось кого-нибудь огорчить.
reading.question: What pleasure did the narrator take when petitioners approached his desk for information?
options: A merciless pleasure whenever he managed to upset someone
reading.correct: A merciless pleasure whenever he managed to upset someone
reading.explain: He describes feeling "merciless pleasure" whenever he succeeded in upsetting a petitioner.

reading.ru: Большую частью все был народ робкий, известный просителем, но из фертов я особенно терпеть не мог одного офицера. Он никак не хотел покориться и омерзительно гремел саблей.
reading.question: Which particular petitioner could the narrator especially not stand?
options: An officer who rattled his saber and refused to submit
reading.correct: An officer who rattled his saber and refused to submit
reading.explain: Among the timid petitioners, he especially could not stand one officer who refused to submit and rattled his saber offensively.

reading.ru: Но, знаете ли, господа, в чем состоял главный пункт моей злости? Да в том и состояла вся штука, в том-то и заключалась наибольшая гадость, что я поминутно, даже в минуту самой сильнейшей желчи, постыдно сознавался себе, что я не только не злой, но даже и не озлобленный человек, что я только воробьев пугаю напрасно и себя этим тешу.
reading.question: What secret truth does the narrator confess about the real point of his malice?
options: That he shamefully realized he was not even truly angry, only scaring sparrows in vain
That his malice was aimed only at his family
That he was proud of his cruelty and never doubted it
That his malice came from genuine hatred of doctors
reading.correct: That he shamefully realized he was not even truly angry, only scaring sparrows in vain
reading.explain: He confesses that even at his angriest, he shamefully knew he was not truly spiteful, just scaring sparrows in vain and amusing himself.

reading.ru: У меня пена во рта, а принесите мне какую-нибудь куколку, дайте мне чайку с сахарцем, я, пожалуй, успокоюсь.
reading.question: What simple things does the narrator say would calm him down even when foaming at the mouth with rage?
options: A little doll and some tea with sugar
reading.correct: A little doll and some tea with sugar
reading.explain: He says that if someone brought him a little doll and some tea with sugar, he would probably calm down.

reading.ru: Я не только злым, но даже и ничем не сумел сделаться. Ни злым, ни добрым, ни подлецом, ни честным, ни героем, ни насекомым.
reading.question: What does the narrator conclude he ultimately failed to become?
options: Anything at all — neither evil, kind, a scoundrel, honest, a hero, nor an insect
reading.correct: Anything at all — neither evil, kind, a scoundrel, honest, a hero, nor an insect
reading.explain: He states he failed to become not only evil but anything at all — not evil, not kind, not a scoundrel, not honest, not a hero, not even an insect.

reading.ru: Даст умный человек 19-го столетия должен и нравственно обязан быть существом по преимуществу бесхарактерным. Человек же с характером – деятель, существом по преимуществу ограниченным.
reading.question: According to the narrator's "conviction," what must an intelligent man of the 19th century be?
reading.correct: A being essentially without character
reading.explain: He argues that an intelligent man of the 19th century is morally obligated to be a being predominantly without character, while a man of character is merely a limited doer.

reading.ru: Мне теперь сорок лет, а ведь сорок лет это вся жизнь, ведь это самая глубокая старость. Дальше сорока лет жить неприлично, пошло, безнравственно.
reading.question: What does the narrator claim about living past the age of forty?
options: It is indecent, vulgar, and immoral
It is the beginning of true wisdom
It is impossible for most people
reading.correct: It is indecent, vulgar, and immoral
reading.explain: He declares that living past forty is "indecent, vulgar, immoral," calling forty the deepest old age.

reading.ru: Я один коллежеский асессор.
reading.question: What official rank does the narrator reveal he holds?
reading.correct: Collegiate assessor
reading.explain: He states plainly, "I am a collegiate assessor."

reading.ru: Когда прошлого года один из отдаленных моих родственников оставил мне 6 тысяч рублей по духовному завещанию, я тут же вышел в отставку и поселился у себя в углу.
reading.question: What allowed the narrator to retire and settle in his corner?
options: Inheriting 6 thousand rubles from a distant relative
reading.correct: Inheriting 6 thousand rubles from a distant relative
reading.explain: He explains that when a distant relative left him 6 thousand rubles by will, he immediately retired and settled in his corner.

reading.ru: Комната моя дренная, скверная, на краю города. Служанка моя деревенская баба, старая, злая от глупости, и от нее к тому же всегда скверно пахнет.
reading.question: How does the narrator describe his room and his servant?
options: A wretched room at the edge of the city, with an old, spiteful peasant servant
A luxurious apartment with several servants
A shared room in a busy dormitory
A cottage in the countryside with no servants
reading.correct: A wretched room at the edge of the city, with an old, spiteful peasant servant
reading.explain: He describes his room as wretched, at the edge of the city, and his servant as an old peasant woman, spiteful from stupidity.

reading.ru: Но я остаюсь в Петербурге. Я не выйду из Петербурга.
reading.question: Despite being told the Petersburg climate is bad for him, what does the narrator decide?
options: He remains in Petersburg and will not leave
He immediately moves to the countryside
He moves in with his relatives
reading.correct: He remains in Petersburg and will not leave
reading.explain: He states firmly, "I remain in Petersburg. I will not leave Petersburg."

reading.ru: Мне теперь хочется рассказать вам, господа, желается или не желается вам это слышать, почему я даже и насекомым не сумел сделаться.
reading.question: What does the narrator want to explain at the start of the second chapter?
options: Why he could not even manage to become an insect
Why he decided to become a doctor
reading.correct: Why he could not even manage to become an insect
reading.explain: He opens chapter two saying he wants to explain why he could not even become an insect.

reading.ru: Скажу вам торжественно, что я много раз хотел сделаться насекомым, но даже и этого не удостоился.
reading.question: What does the narrator solemnly admit he wanted to become many times, but never achieved?
reading.correct: An insect
reading.explain: He solemnly declares he wanted many times to become an insect, but did not even achieve that.

reading.ru: До того доходил, что ощущал какое-то тайное, ненормальное, подлинное наслаждение с возвращаться.
reading.question: What secret, shameful pleasure did the narrator feel upon returning to his corner after doing something bad?
options: A secret, abnormal, genuine pleasure in that awareness
Pure regret with no pleasure at all
Complete indifference to what he had done
A desire to confess immediately to others
reading.correct: A secret, abnormal, genuine pleasure in that awareness
reading.explain: He admits he felt a secret, abnormal, genuine pleasure returning to his corner aware that he had again done something base.

reading.ru: Я, например, ужасно самолюбив. Я мнительен и обивчив, как горбун или карлик.
reading.question: How does the narrator describe his own vanity and sensitivity?
options: Terribly vain, and as touchy as a hunchback or a dwarf
reading.correct: Terribly vain, and as touchy as a hunchback or a dwarf
reading.explain: He confesses he is terribly vain (self-loving), and as suspicious and touchy as a hunchback or a dwarf.

reading.ru: Но, право, бывали со мной такие минуты, что если бы случилось, что мне бы дали пощечину, то, может быть, я был бы даже рад этому.
reading.question: What surprising reaction does the narrator imagine he might have if he were slapped in the face?
options: He might even be glad of it
reading.correct: He might even be glad of it
reading.explain: He says that in certain moments, if he were given a slap, he might even be glad of it.

reading.ru: Во-первых, виноват, что я умнее всех, которые меня окружают. Я постоянно считал себя умнее всех, которые меня окружают.
reading.question: What does the narrator constantly believe about himself in relation to those around him?
options: That he is smarter than everyone who surrounds him
That he is far less intelligent than others
That he is exactly as intelligent as everyone else
That intelligence does not matter to him
reading.correct: That he is smarter than everyone who surrounds him
reading.explain: He admits he constantly considered himself smarter than everyone around him.

reading.ru: Не простить, потому что обидчик, может, ударил меня по законам природы, а законов природы нельзя прощать. Не забыть, потому что хоть законы природы, а все-таки обидно.
reading.question: Why does the narrator say he could neither forgive nor forget an offender?
options: Because the offender acted by the laws of nature, which cannot be forgiven, yet it is still offensive and cannot be forgotten
Because he never actually gets offended by anyone
Because forgiveness is against his religion
Because he always seeks immediate revenge instead
reading.correct: Because the offender acted by the laws of nature, which cannot be forgiven, yet it is still offensive and cannot be forgotten
reading.explain: He reasons he cannot forgive because the offender acted by the laws of nature (which cannot be forgiven), and cannot forget because, laws of nature or not, it is still offensive.
